Roman Catholic parishes fell under the Diocese of Philadelphia until the Diocese of Scranton was erected in 1868; sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; pre-1906 events are recorded in church, cemetery, and probate records instead.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) -- browse image-by-image.

items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been searched. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

items.guide_markdown:
## Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania - 1838-1900

Schuylkill County (formed 1811 from Berks and Northampton) lies in Pennsylvania's anthracite coal region. Probate is held by the county Register of Wills from 1811. Catholic parishes moved from the Diocese of Philadelphia to the Diocese of Scranton in 1868. Statewide civil vital registration began only in 1906, so pre-1906 vital events depend on church, cemetery, and probate records. Some coal-region naturalization and church films are browse-only.

entry.rationale: Exhaustive search for all children of Bridget Halloran and John Doyle in Schuylkill County, PA. Ellen Doyle is the one already-identified child. Strategy: (1) enumerate family across all available federal census years to capture children present at each snapshot; (2) search indexed and browse-only church baptism registers (Catholic parishes fell under Philadelphia Diocese until 1868, then Scranton Diocese — civil registration did not begin until 1906); (3) browse John Doyle's probate estate, which would name heirs by law; (4) examine children's marriage records for parental names; (5) use Ellen Doyle as a FAN anchor — her adult records may name parents and surviving siblings. Name variants to test throughout: Doil, Doyel, Doyal. Collections identified: SYNTH-PA-CHURCH (indexed, 982,415 persons); US census collections 1473181/1438024/1417683/1325221 (all indexed); Ancestry collection 1276 for 1850; browse-only image groups 007936749 (probate), 007936751 (church), 007936753 (marriage); Pennsylvania Probate collection 1999196 (browse-only). Standard place: Schuylkill, Pennsylvania, United States.

United States Census 1880 (collection 1417683, indexed, 50.2M persons). The 1880 census is the highest-priority household source because it explicitly records each member's relationship to the head of household — uniquely reliable for enumerating children still at home. Search for John Doyle and for Bridget Halloran/Doyle in Schuylkill County. Include name variants Doil, Doyel. Any child listed in the household with relationship 'son' or 'daughter' is direct evidence. Also search for the household of Ellen Doyle (known child) to identify whether she was co-resident with siblings.

United States Census 1860 (collection 1473181, indexed, 27.5M persons). An earlier household snapshot captures children born before 1860 who may have left home by 1880. The 1860 census does not record relationships, but children enumerated contiguously with the parents in age-descending order can be inferred. Search John Doyle in Schuylkill County with variants Doil, Doyel. Children identified here but absent in 1880 may have died, married, or migrated.

United States Census 1870 (collection 1438024, indexed, 38.6M persons). Mid-period snapshot bridging the 1860 and 1880 censuses. Older children who left the household by 1880 may still appear in 1870. Like 1860, does not record explicit relationships — household proximity and age sequence carry the inference. Search John Doyle and Bridget Halloran in Schuylkill County; variants Doil, Doyel.

1850 United States Federal Census — Schuylkill County (Ancestry collection 1276, identified via external_links_search). The 1850 census is not available as an indexed FamilySearch collection for this county and must be accessed via Ancestry. The earliest household snapshot — captures children born before 1850 who may not appear at all in later censuses if they died young or migrated. John Doyle's 1850 household could reveal the oldest Doyle children. Note: 1850 census does not record names of persons under one year, and does not name relationships — age and household position carry the inference.

United States Census 1900 (collection 1325221, indexed, 76.2M persons). By 1900 the Doyle children would be adults, likely heading their own households. The 1900 census records mother's number of children born and surviving — a direct enumeration aid. Search for Doyle-surnamed households in Schuylkill County (and adjacent counties for out-migrants) whose members' ages and parents' birthplaces are consistent with John and Bridget. Also search for Bridget Halloran/Doyle as a widow living with adult children, which would name the child she resided with. Variants Doil, Doyel.

Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records (collection SYNTH-PA-CHURCH, indexed, 982,415 persons, date range 1708–1985). Pennsylvania had no civil birth registration before 1906; Catholic baptism registers are the primary record of children's births. Catholic parishes in this anthracite region fell under the Diocese of Philadelphia until 1868 and the Diocese of Scranton thereafter. Search for baptisms of children with surname Doyle (variants: Doil, Doyel) and parents named John Doyle and Bridget Halloran/Doyle. A baptism entry naming both parents directly establishes the child's parentage. This indexed collection covers many Schuylkill County parishes and is the most efficient entry point.

Schuylkill County Church Records, browse-only image group 007936749 (187 images, 0% record-searchable, languages: en, de, covering 1842–1895). volume_search confirmed this group is not indexed — access requires paging through images. This group may cover parishes or registers not captured in the indexed SYNTH-PA-CHURCH collection, including German-language Catholic registers in the coal-region. Browse for Doyle baptism entries in the relevant date window. Per the locality guide, some coal-region church films are browse-only; this is one such group. Fallback for item 6 (pli_006) for parishes absent from the indexed collection.

Schuylkill County Probate Records, browse-only image group 007936749 (412 images, 0% record-searchable, covering 1851–1930). Also Pennsylvania Probate Records 1683–1994 (collection 1999196, personCount 0 — browse-only). Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills from 1811 per the locality guide. A will by John Doyle would name heirs, which under intestacy law would include all surviving children — direct parentage evidence. Bridget's own probate (if she outlived John) could similarly name children. Date range set to 1838–1920 to cover the plausible lifespans of both John and Bridget, whose death dates are unknown. Browse the docket index for Doyle entries (variants Doil, Doyel). This is a high-value source for a completeness question because a will naming 'my children' or listing specific heirs enumerates all who were alive at the testator's death.

Schuylkill County Marriage Records, browse-only image group 007936753 (94 images, 0% record-searchable, covering 1870–1910). When Doyle children married, the marriage register would record both spouses' names and typically their parents' names — direct parentage evidence for each marrying child. Browse for entries with groom or bride surname Doyle (variants Doil, Doyel) and a parent named John Doyle or Bridget Halloran. Date range reflects children born in the 1840s–1880s reaching marrying age. This source is especially valuable for daughters who would not retain the Doyle surname after marriage, making them invisible to surname searches in later records.

FAN pivot on Ellen Doyle (I3), the one already-identified child of John and Bridget. Ellen's adult records serve as a bridge to her siblings: (a) her death certificate, if she died after Pennsylvania's 1906 civil registration began, would name her parents (Bridget Halloran and John Doyle) and the informant — likely a sibling — identifying another Doyle child by name; (b) her census appearances as an adult (1870–1910) may show her co-residing with or near siblings; (c) her marriage record (browse-only 007936753, or indexed church records) would name her parents, confirming the connection and potentially showing a witness who is a sibling. Search FamilySearch indexed collections for Ellen Doyle in Schuylkill County across census years; check post-1906 Pennsylvania vital records for her death certificate.
